parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Light of wavelength λ₀ ejects electrons from a metal of work function Φ. Derive their maximum speed in terms of λ₀, Φ, Planck’s constant h, the speed of light c and electron mass m_e. Predict how that maximum speed changes if the wavelength is increased but emission still occurs, and explain why.

answer.text: Photon energy is hc/λ₀. Einstein’s photoelectric equation gives ½m_e v_max² = hc/λ₀ − Φ, so v_max = √[(2/m_e)(hc/λ₀ − Φ)]. Increasing wavelength lowers photon energy. With the same work function, less energy remains as maximum electron kinetic energy, so the maximum speed decreases.

A photoelectric experiment illuminates a polished metal surface. The first graph shows collected current against opposing potential difference for incident frequency 2.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz. The second shows stopping-potential magnitude V_s against frequency. Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

answer.text:
(a) Electrons are emitted from a material when incident electromagnetic radiation supplies sufficient energy.
(b) A photon has energy hf. After work function Φ is overcome, K_max = hf − Φ = eV_s. Higher frequency therefore gives a greater stopping potential.
(c) Examples: threshold frequency ≈ 1.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz; graph gradient h/e ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s, giving h ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; work function hf₀ ≈ 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 6.2 eV. At zero opposing voltage the collected current is about 2.7 mA, corresponding to about 1.7 × 10¹⁶ collected electrons per second.

(a)(i) Identify graph features corresponding to A and B; explain their physical meanings and f₀. (ii) Explain the horizontal section below f₀. (ii) Explain why green light does not. (c) If green-light intensity increases to equal the UV intensity, what property changes and will the leaves move?

answer.text: A is the graph slope and equals Planck’s constant h. B is the positive work function Φ (the K-axis intercept is −B); f₀=Φ/h is the threshold frequency. A second metal keeps the same slope h but can have a different threshold/intercept. UV photons with hf≥Φ eject electrons, leaving the electroscope less negative so its leaves converge. Green photons have hf<Φ, so none eject electrons. Increasing intensity raises photon arrival rate (and wave amplitude), not energy per photon, so even equally intense green light still causes no emission. Below threshold, the source’s horizontal line signifies no photoelectrons emitted, rather than electrons with negative kinetic energy. For a second metal of larger work function, shift the rising section right while keeping it parallel (slope h), so f₀ is larger.

answer.text: Official markscheme result: v_max=1.5×10⁶ m s⁻¹. Editorial worked explanation: The maximum kinetic energy is K_max=E_photon−Φ=1.63×10⁻¹⁸−5.89×10⁻¹⁹=1.041×10⁻¹⁸ J. Thus v_max=√(2K_max/m_e)=√[2(1.041×10⁻¹⁸)/(9.11×10⁻³¹)]=1.51×10⁶ m s⁻¹. The observations are explained by quantized photons: there is a threshold frequency because one photon must provide at least the work function; emission is effectively immediate; and increasing intensity increases photon number rather than the maximum energy delivered in one photon–electron interaction. Each photon transfers its energy to one electron, behavior inconsistent with energy arriving continuously from a classical wave.

Published key A checked; editorial worked explanation:

A threshold frequency follows because a single photon below the work-function energy cannot release an electron, regardless of how many such photons arrive per second.

cross-fast-ocr-9b5d09d08cd2c050-3-whole:.hint: Compare the scale of the wave with the spacing that produces an observable diffraction pattern.
notes: Diffraction is strongest when wavelength and obstacle or lattice spacing have comparable scales.
The de Broglie relation supplies a wavelength for electrons, so electron diffraction is evidence for matter-wave behavior.

cross-fast-ocr-9b5d09d08cd2c050-8-whole:.hint: Separate the unconditional single-photon law from claims about electron rate, which also require intensity or photon-flux conditions.
notes: At fixed frequency, increasing intensity increases photon arrival rate rather than the energy carried by each photon.
A threshold frequency and immediate emission support quantized photon interactions rather than continuous wave-energy accumulation.

cross-fast-ocr-9b5d09d08cd2c050-23-photo.hint: Use E=hf for the threshold and photon energy. At fixed frequency, translate intensity into photon rate, then photon rate into collected-electron current.
notes: The proportionality between photocurrent and intensity assumes fixed frequency above threshold, so photon energy does not vary during the comparison.
The numerical estimate is ideal: it assumes every incident photon ejects one electron and every emitted electron is collected.

cross-fast-production-006-a-q12:whole.hint: Convert the work function to joules, subtract it from the photon energy, then use the electron kinetic-energy equation.
notes: The photon energy and work function must use the same unit before subtraction; 1 eV is 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ J.
The photoelectric equation gives the maximum emitted-electron kinetic energy, which is then converted to speed using ½mₑv².

cross-fast-production-006-a-q13:whole.hint: Relate particle kinetic energy to de Broglie wavelength, then relate wavelength and screen geometry to the ring radius.
notes: At fixed particle mass, reducing kinetic energy reduces momentum and therefore increases the de Broglie wavelength.
A larger lattice spacing reduces the diffraction angle for a fixed wavelength, while moving the screen closer reduces every ring radius.

cross-fast-production-007-a-a16:whole.hint: Separate photon arrival rate from the energy carried by each photon.
notes: Intensity at fixed frequency changes photon flux and electron emission rate.
Maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency and work function, not flux.

cross-fast-production-007-a-a19:whole.hint: Recall which particle property determines the de Broglie wavelength.
notes: Charge affects motion in fields but does not explain diffraction fringes.
Greater momentum produces shorter matter wavelength through λ=h/p.

cross-fast-production-007-a-b15-a:whole.hint: Use stopping potential for photon energy and saturation current for photon rate.
notes: Equal saturation current fixes electron rate, not energy flux.

notes: The non-relativistic momentum approximation is valid at this speed.
